Introduction
The N400 is a negative-going ERP component that typically peaks around 400 milliseconds after the onset of a stimulus. It is most prominently observed at central and parietal electrode sites (Cz, Pz) and is characterised by its centroparietal topographic distribution.

Discovery and Basic Characteristics
The N400 was first described by @kutas1980 in a landmark study that examined brain responses to semantically incongruent words in sentences. In their seminal work, Kutas and Hillyard presented participants with sentences ending in either semantically appropriate words or unexpected words. They observed a large negative deflection peaking around 400ms for semantically incongruent endings, hence the name "N400."

Key characteristics of the N400:

Polarity: Negative
Latency: 250-500ms post-stimulus (peaks ~400ms)
Topography: Maximal at centroparietal electrodes (Cz, Pz)
Amplitude: Typically 5-8 µV in linguistic contexts
Functional Significance
The N400 has been extensively studied as an index of semantic processing. Research has demonstrated that the N400 amplitude varies with:

Semantic incongruity: Larger N400 for unexpected or incongruent words
Cloze probability: Words with lower probability of completing a sentence elicit larger N400s [@kutas1984]
Semantic relatedness: Unrelated word pairs elicit larger N400s than related pairs [@bentin1985]
Controversies
While the N400 is widely accepted as a measure of semantic processing, its precise functional interpretation remains debated:

Some researchers argue it reflects lexical access processes
Others propose it indexes semantic integration in context
Recent work suggests it may reflect prediction mechanisms in language processing [@kuperberg2016]

## Methods

Complete the following subsections using the information from @kappenman2021. Don't forget to mention that the data are from the ERP CORE resource under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-SA 4.0). 

### Participants

40 neurologically healthy adults (20 female, 20 male) participated in the study. Participants ranged in age from 18 to 30 years (mean age = 21.5 years, SD = 2.6). All participants were right-handed, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and were native English speakers. Participants gave informed consent prior to the study. The data are from the ERP CORE resource [@kappenman2021] under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-SA 4.0).

### Procedure

Participants completed a semantic judgement task in which they were presented with pairs of words. The critical manipulation involved the semantic relationship between word pairs:

Related condition: Semantically related word pairs (e.g., "bread - butter")
Unrelated condition: Semantically unrelated word pairs (e.g., "bread - doctor")
Each trial consisted of:

Fixation cross (500ms)
Prime word (200ms)
Inter-stimulus interval (300ms)
Target word (displayed until response)
Participants indicated whether each target word was a real word or a non-word via button press.

### EEG recording

EEG was recorded using the following parameters [@kappenman2021]:

Amplifier: BrainVision actiCHamp
Cap: Brain Products actiCAP
Electrode positions: 30 active electrodes placed according to the 10-20 system
CMS/DRL electrodes: Located at P9/P10 (used as reference)
EOG electrodes:
Horizontal EOG: Lateral to each eye
Vertical EOG: Above and below the left eye
Filter parameters:
Online: DC to 80 Hz
Offline: 0.1 Hz (high-pass) to 30 Hz (low-pass)

### Analysis parameters

Choose these parameters appropriate for the component that you are analysing. Use those recommended by @kappenman2021; see their Table 1. This holds for all parameters except for the filter parameters; for these, you can stick to the example parameters provided below.
Describe the parameters in this section and also modify the code accordingly

#### Preprocessing parameters

FILTER_SETTINGS = {
    "low_cutoff": 0.1,   # High-pass filter at 0.1 Hz
    "high_cutoff": 30.0  # Low-pass filter at 30 Hz
}

# Reference to averaged mastoids (P9/P10 as proxy)
REFERENCE = ["P9", "P10"]

#### Epoching parameters

# N400 specific parameters based on Kappenman et al. (2021)
TMIN = -0.2    # 200ms pre-stimulus baseline
TMAX = 0.8     # 800ms post-stimulus

BASELINE = (-0.2, 0)  # 200ms pre-stimulus baseline correction

# N400 conditions: related vs unrelated word pairs
CONDITIONS = ["stimulus/unrelated", "stimulus/related"]

# Artifact rejection thresholds
REJECT = {
    "eeg": 150e-6,   # 150 µV for EEG channels
    "eog": 250e-6    # 250 µV for EOG channels
}

```

## Data analysis

### Preprocessing


#| eval: true
#| output: true

# Find EEG files
raw_files = sorted(RAW_PATH.glob("*_raw.fif.gz"))
print(f"Found {len(raw_files)} EEG files", flush=True)

for raw_file in raw_files:
    print(f"\nProcessing: {raw_file.name}", flush=True)
    
    # Extract subject ID
    subj_ID = raw_file.name.split("_")[0]
    
    # Define output path
    output_file = PROCESSED_PATH / f"{subj_ID}_raw.fif.gz"
    
    # Skip if already processed
    if output_file.exists():
        print(f"Already processed, skipping: {raw_file.name}", flush=True)
        continue
    
    try:
        # Read raw file
        raw = SimpleRaw(raw_file)
        print("EEG file loaded successfully", flush=True)
        
        # Preprocess
        processed = preprocess(
            raw,
            reref_params=REFERENCE,
            filter_low_cutoff=FILTER_SETTINGS["low_cutoff"],
            filter_high_cutoff=FILTER_SETTINGS["high_cutoff"]
        )
        print("Preprocessing completed", flush=True)
        
        # Create processed directory if needed
        PROCESSED_PATH.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        
        # Save processed data
        processed.save(
            output_file,
            overwrite=True
        )
        print(f"Saved: {output_file.name}", flush=True)
        
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error processing {raw_file.name}: {e}", flush=True)
        continue

print("\nPreprocessing complete!", flush=True)

```

### Grand average

#| eval: true
#| output: false

# Compute grand averages for each condition
grand_avs = {}

for cond in CONDITIONS:
    if len(ss_avs[cond]) == 0:
        print(f"Warning: No data available for condition: {cond}")
        continue
    
    print(
        f"Computing grand average for {cond}: "
        f"n={len(ss_avs[cond])} participants"
    )
    
    grand = grand_average(ss_avs[cond])
    grand_avs[cond] = grand

print("Grand averages computed successfully!")
```

## Results

Grand Average: N400 Effect
#| eval: true
#| output: true

# N400 analysis parameters based on Kappenman et al. (2021)
# Representative electrode: Pz (centroparietal maximum)
selected_electrode = "Pz"

# N400 analysis window: 300-500ms
analysis_window_start = 0.3
analysis_window_end = 0.5

plot_title = (
    "Grand Average N400: "
    "Unrelated vs. Related Word Pairs at Pz"
)

# Plot grand averages
plot_evokeds(
    grand_avs,
    picks=selected_electrode,
    invert_y=True,          # Negative up (convention for ERPs)
    title=plot_title,
    vlines=[
        analysis_window_start, 
        analysis_window_end
    ]
) 
The grand average ERP at electrode Pz reveals the expected N400 effect. The unrelated word pairs condition shows a more negative deflection compared to the related word pairs condition in the 300-500ms time window, consistent with the N400 component described by @kappenman2021.
```

## Discussion and reflection

Results Summary
The grand average ERP analysis revealed a clear N400 effect at the centroparietal electrode site Pz. The unrelated word pairs condition elicited a more pronounced negative deflection between 300-500ms post-stimulus compared to the related word pairs condition. This pattern is consistent with the classic N400 effect reported by @kutas1980 and replicated by @kappenman2021.

Comparison with Kappenman et al. (2021)
The observed N400 effect aligns with the findings reported by @kappenman2021 in terms of:

Polarity: Negative deflection as expected
Latency: Peak around 400ms post-stimulus
Topography: Maximal at centroparietal sites
Minor differences in amplitude may be attributable to individual differences in the participant sample or slight variations in task parameters.

Reflections on Learning
Applying the ERP analysis pipeline to a new dataset provided valuable insights into:

Pipeline implementation: Understanding how preprocessing steps (filtering, re-referencing, artifact rejection) influence the final ERP waveform
Parameter selection: The importance of selecting appropriate epoch windows and rejection thresholds for specific components
Data quality: Recognising how artifact rejection affects the number of valid trials per participant
Reproducibility: The value of structured, documented code for ensuring reproducible analyses
